title: Parabolas: one distance rule, five checkable steps

script.title: Parabolas: one distance rule, five checkable steps

beats.say: Champ, a parabola can be built from one simple rule. Choose a fixed point, called the focus, and a fixed line, called the directrix.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A parabola is the set of all points equally far from that point and that line. Distance to a line means the shortest distance: straight to it at a right angle.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.meaning: All points equally far from a fixed focus and a fixed directrix.

beats.say: So I can choose any point on the line to measure to?
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Which point on the line gives the shortest distance?

beats.say: Use the nearest point, D, directly below P. Here the slant to the focus and the drop to the directrix both measure two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Move P along this curve. Its two distances change together. At four, four, each is five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: That equal-distance rule survives every move. An equation describes all those locations at once.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: One geometric rule → an equation for the whole curve.

beats.say: Let P have coordinates x, y: x across, y up. For a general focus a, b, the horizontal and vertical changes form a right triangle.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The Pythagorean theorem says the hypotenuse squared is the sum of the leg squares. Distance to the focus is the nonnegative square root of that sum.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Pythagorean theorem: add the two leg squares.

beats.say: For a horizontal directrix, y equals d, only the vertical difference matters. Its distance is the absolute value of y minus d.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Why the absolute value?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: A distance cannot be negative. From height one to height five, one minus five is negative four, but the distance is four.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Subtract the given coordinate, including its sign: $y-(-2)=y+2$.

beats.say: For a vertical directrix, x equals c, measure horizontally instead. Its distance is the absolute value of x minus c.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Focus: two coordinate differences. Line: one perpendicular difference.

beats.say: Now derive a complete equation. The focus is one, six, and the directrix is y equals negative two. Every line has a job.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line one states the definition. Distance to the focus equals distance to the directrix.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line two squares both sides. The square root disappears, and the absolute value squared becomes the ordinary square.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Square the entire right side too.

beats.say: Does squaring ever add solutions?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: It can when signs differ. Here both sides are distances, so both are nonnegative. For nonnegative quantities, equality of their squares is equivalent to equality of the quantities.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Both sides are nonnegative distances: squaring gains or loses no points.

beats.say: Line three expands the two y squares. Keep x minus one squared intact; it will survive in the answer.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line four subtracts y squared from both sides. Add twelve y and subtract thirty-six on both sides. Four y plus twelve y is sixteen y; four minus thirty-six is negative thirty-two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line five factors sixteen from the entire right side. Negative thirty-two divided by sixteen is negative two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: To justify a marked step, name exactly what changed. Two to three: expand. Three to four: subtract y squared and collect. Four to five: factor sixteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Reasons describe operations, not merely the appearance of a line.

beats.say: The geometry gives us a quick independent check. The vertex is the point on the curve halfway between the focus and the directrix, along their perpendicular axis.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check the equation against the geometry.

beats.say: Here the focus has height six, and the directrix has height negative two. The midpoint height is two. So the vertex is one, two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Let p be the signed coordinate change from vertex to focus: positive up or right, negative down or left. Here p is four.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Up or right: $p>0$. Down or left: $p<0$.

beats.say: Why does the equation use four p?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Measure from vertex h, k using X across and Y up. The focus is at height p and the directrix at height negative p. Square the equal distances, then expand.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The matching squares cancel. Moving negative two p Y to the right adds another two p Y. That leaves four p Y.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The full focus-to-directrix gap is eight. The vertex-to-focus distance is half of that, four. So four p is sixteen, not thirty-two.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: $|p|$ is HALF the focus–directrix gap. Keep the sign of $p$.

beats.say: A vertical directrix makes the parabola open sideways. Here the focus is negative two, four, and the directrix is x equals negative six.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The vertex is halfway across, at negative four, four. The focus lies to its right, so the curve opens right.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The distance to the line is horizontal this time: absolute value of x plus six.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: So the x squares will cancel, and the y square will survive?
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: The $x^2$ terms cancel; the $y$ square survives.

beats.say: Exactly. A horizontal directrix leaves an x square; a vertical directrix leaves a y square. Follow the distances to choose which.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: The uncanceled square tells the orientation.

beats.say: Let's finish the sideways derivation and practice naming reasons.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line one comes from the equal-distance definition of a parabola.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Square both nonnegative sides for line two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Expand x plus two squared and x plus six squared for line three.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Subtract x squared, four x, and four from both sides. Twelve x minus four x is eight x. Thirty-six minus four is thirty-two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Factor eight from both terms on the right.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: For the marked steps two to three and three to four, I'd choose expand, then subtract x squared and collect.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Yes. In the sideways form, p is the focus's x coordinate minus the vertex's x coordinate. Negative two minus negative four is two, so four p is eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Negative p means the focus is below or left of the vertex. Here the focus is negative six, three, and the directrix is x equals negative two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Write equal distances and square both sides.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Expand the x squares.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Cancel x squared, then subtract twelve x and thirty-six. Four x minus twelve x is negative eight x; four minus thirty-six is negative thirty-two.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Factor negative eight. The constant inside becomes positive four, because negative thirty-two divided by negative eight is four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The midpoint is negative four, three. From there to the focus is two units left: p equals negative two. Four p equals negative eight.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Positive $p$: up or right. Negative $p$: down or left.

beats.say: Now check someone else's work. Start with the actual givens, before trusting any algebra. Focus negative three, negative one; directrix x equals negative five.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The student's first line is shown. Which distance uses the wrong coordinate?
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Pause: compare the focus inside the root with the given focus.

beats.say: The root measures to negative five, negative one. But the focus is negative three, negative one. They swapped the focus's x coordinate with the directrix!
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: The root uses $(-5,-1)$, not the given focus.
Focus and directrix coordinates were swapped.

beats.say: Correct. The two focus coordinates belong inside the root. The directrix coordinate belongs in the one-coordinate distance on the right.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Later algebra could follow perfectly from the wrong first line. Stop here: the question asks for the first incorrect line.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check Line 1 against the givens. Check every later line against its predecessor.
Stop at the first invalid line.

beats.say: Two different mistakes can occur when handling the square root. Use focus zero, one, and directrix y equals negative one.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The correct first line is the square root of x squared plus y minus one squared, equal to absolute value of y plus one.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: One square root covers the WHOLE sum.

beats.say: Could I split that root into absolute x plus absolute y minus one?
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: No. The root of a sum is not generally the sum of the roots. A three-four-five right triangle makes it visible: the slant is five, while three plus four is seven.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A different student keeps the sum, but squares only the left side. Is this line valid?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Both sides need the same operation. The right side must be y plus one squared.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Exactly. Splitting a root and squaring one side are different errors. Name the one the student actually made.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Square the whole left side AND the whole right side.
Name the error in the actual transition.

beats.say: Expansion is another common trouble spot. This example uses focus six, negative four, and directrix y equals negative six.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Lines one and two correctly state equal distances and square both sides.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The student writes this third line. What is missing?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The twelve y on the right!
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Yes. Squaring a binomial means multiplying the entire pair by itself. Each cross product contributes six y.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: So the first error is line three: the middle term was dropped. The correct expansion gives the correct final equation.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The student's later lines might be valid algebra from the faulty expansion. They carry the error forward; they do not change where it began.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: $(u-v)^2=u^2-2uv+v^2$: the constant square is positive; the middle term keeps its sign.

beats.say: Check cancellation by doing the same operation on both sides. Use focus negative five, negative one, and directrix y equals five.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Check the move from Line 3 to Line 4.

beats.say: The first two lines use the correct distances and square both sides.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line three expands correctly. But the student's line four has a sign error.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: I see negative ten y plus two y makes negative eight y.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: That would add two y on the right without removing it on the left. To remove positive two y, subtract two y from both sides. Negative ten y minus two y is negative twelve y.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Repair Line 4 by subtracting from BOTH sides.

beats.say: The answer is line four, with the sign unchanged when the term was moved. Thinking subtract from both sides makes the sign automatic.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Use the same subtraction on both sides.

beats.say: Return to our upward example. These first four lines are all correct. Check each transition, then inspect the final line.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The distances are correct, both sides are squared, and both y squares are expanded.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Cancel and collect to get sixteen y minus thirty-two. But line five uses thirty-two outside the parentheses.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The vertex is right, so is it okay?
beats.speaker: learner

do.text: Is the vertex alone enough to check the curve?

beats.say: The vertex alone does not determine the curve. Distribute thirty-two: it gives thirty-two y minus sixty-four, which is not line four.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The first error is line five: the outside factor should be sixteen. The geometry agrees: the gap is eight, p is four, and four p is sixteen.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The same error sideways would change four times x minus three into eight times x minus three. Expanding back catches it immediately.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A different factoring mistake changes the number inside the parentheses. Focus negative five, negative one; directrix y equals five. The first four lines are correct.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Opening down: check the constant inside the factor.

beats.say: The correct distances, squaring, and expansion give these lines.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: After canceling and collecting, the right side is negative twelve y plus twenty-four. The student factors it as negative twelve times y minus four.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Factor each term, including the constant.

beats.say: Twenty-four divided by negative twelve is negative two, not negative four.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Yes. Divide every term by the factor. Then distribute back to check.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: The vertex has height two, halfway between negative one and five. The focus is three units below it, so p is negative three. That confirms negative twelve and opening down.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: A midpoint can be a fraction. With focus four, negative three, and directrix y equals negative four, the midpoint height is negative three point five. Then p is one half.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Fractional vertex coordinates and fractional $p$ are valid.

beats.say: Try a reason question yourself. Focus negative one, five; directrix x equals negative three. Every line here is correct.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Choose the reasons for Line 1 and for Line 4 → Line 5.

beats.say: Read the five lines. Why is line one true, and what changes from line four to line five?
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: Line one is the equal-distance definition. Four to five factors four from the right side.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Exactly. It does not divide both sides by four: the left side has not changed. A reason must describe the actual transition.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Compare the two marked lines. Name the operation that actually happened.

beats.say: Check a derivation with these four steps.
beats.speaker: teacher

beats.say: First, build the equal-distance equation from the given focus and directrix.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Build equal distances from the givens.

beats.say: Redo each transition in order. Stop at the first invalid step.
beats.speaker: teacher

do.text: Square, expand, collect, factor. Stop at the first error.

beats.say: For a reason question, name the operation between the two marked lines.
beats.speaker: learner

beats.say: Check the midpoint vertex, opening toward the focus, and coefficient four p.
beats.speaker: teacher
